concepts.name: What Is Science?
concepts.description: Science is a way of understanding the world around us. It is not just a collection of facts — it is a way of thinking, observing, and finding out by doing. Asking questions like 'why' and 'how', and looking for evidence-based answers, is at the heart of being a scientist. Cooking, gardening, fixing things, even playing — all these involve scientific thinking.

concepts.name: Asking Questions and Exploring
concepts.description: Curiosity drives science. Scientists notice something interesting, ask questions, make a guess (hypothesis), test it through observations or experiments, and look at the results. Mistakes and unexpected results are valuable — they teach us something new. Doing science also means working together, sharing what we find, and building on each other's ideas. The journey of science is about exploring, not just memorising.

concepts.name: Diversity in Plants and Animals Around Us
concepts.description: The world around us has an enormous variety of plants and animals. They differ in size, shape, colour, where they live, and how they move and feed. By observing carefully, we can spot many differences and similarities — a sparrow, a butterfly, a peepal tree, and a cat are all very different yet all alive. This rich variety is called biodiversity.

concepts.name: How to Group Plants and Animals?
concepts.description: Sorting things into groups makes them easier to study. Plants can be grouped by size and structure: herbs (small soft stems like mint, grass), shrubs (medium woody plants like rose), trees (tall with hard trunks like mango), creepers (lie on the ground like pumpkin), and climbers (use support like money plant). Animals can be grouped by where they live, what they eat, or how they move.

concepts.name: Plants and Animals in Different Surroundings
concepts.description: Different plants and animals live in different surroundings — these surroundings are called habitats. A camel lives in the desert; a fish lives in water; a polar bear lives in icy regions. Each living thing has special features (adaptations) that help it survive in its habitat: thick fur in cold places, fins for swimming, deep roots in dry places. Habitats can be terrestrial (land) or aquatic (water).

units.name: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body

concepts.name: What Do We Eat?
concepts.description: We eat many different foods every day. Food gives us energy to move, helps our body grow, and keeps us healthy. The food we eat comes mainly from plants (rice, wheat, dal, vegetables, fruits) and animals (milk, eggs, fish, meat). Different parts of plants are edible — roots (carrot), stems (potato), leaves (spinach), fruits (mango), and seeds (rice).

concepts.name: What are the Components of Food?
concepts.description: Food is made up of nutrients that the body needs. The main nutrients are: carbohydrates (give energy — rice, wheat, potato), proteins (build and repair the body — dal, eggs, milk), fats (store energy — ghee, butter, nuts), vitamins (protect from disease — fruits, vegetables), and minerals (needed in small amounts — calcium, iron). Water and roughage (dietary fibre) are also essential.

concepts.name: How to Test Different Components of Food?
concepts.description: Simple tests can detect nutrients in food. Iodine test: turns blue-black with starch (carbohydrates). Paper test: a fat sample leaves a translucent (greasy) spot on paper. Protein test: copper sulphate + caustic soda solution turns violet in the presence of protein. These tests are easy to do and show that even everyday foods contain measurable nutrients.

concepts.name: Balanced Diet
concepts.description: A balanced diet contains all nutrients in the right proportions — carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water, and fibre. It keeps us healthy, gives us energy, and helps the body grow. The right amount varies by age, gender, and activity. Eating too much of one nutrient or too little of another causes deficiency diseases (e.g., night blindness, scurvy, anaemia, goitre). Mindful eating means choosing food that is healthy and not wasted.

concepts.name: Millets: Nutrition-rich Cereals
concepts.description: Millets like jowar, bajra, ragi, and sanwa are traditional Indian cereals. They are rich in protein, fibre, iron, and calcium. They grow well even in dry regions with little water and few fertilisers, making them climate-friendly. The United Nations declared 2023 as the International Year of Millets to revive their use. Adding millets to the diet helps both health and the environment.

concepts.name: Food Miles: From Farm to Our Plate
concepts.description: Food miles is the distance food travels from where it is grown to our plate. Eating local and seasonal food reduces food miles, supports nearby farmers, and saves fuel and packaging. Long-distance food (apples from another country, packaged snacks) uses more energy and adds to pollution. Buying from local markets and reducing food waste are simple ways to help the planet.

concepts.name: Magnetic and Non-magnetic Materials
concepts.description: A magnet attracts certain materials called magnetic materials — mainly iron, nickel, and cobalt. Materials that are not attracted are non-magnetic — like aluminium, copper, wood, plastic, rubber, and glass. Steel (an alloy of iron) is magnetic. This property is used to separate magnetic materials from waste, like iron filings from sand.

concepts.name: Poles of a Magnet
concepts.description: Every magnet has two poles — North (N) and South (S). The pull of a magnet is strongest at the poles. Iron filings sprinkled around a bar magnet collect mostly at the ends, showing where the poles are. Even a tiny piece of a broken magnet has both N and S poles — you can never get a magnet with only one pole.

concepts.name: Finding Directions
concepts.description: A freely suspended magnet always points along the North-South direction. This is because the Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet. A magnetic compass is a small magnetic needle that pivots freely; the red (or marked) end points to geographic North. Compasses help travellers, hikers, ships, and pilots find their way. Smartphones also use digital compasses based on the same idea.

concepts.name: Attraction and Repulsion between Magnets
concepts.description: Like poles of magnets repel each other (N and N push away, S and S push away). Unlike poles attract each other (N and S pull together). This is the rule of magnetic interaction. We can test it by bringing two bar magnets near each other slowly and feeling the push or pull. Repulsion is the surest test that an object is a magnet.

concepts.name: Fun with Magnets
concepts.description: Magnets are used in many objects we use daily — fridge magnets, the speakers in earphones and TVs, electric motors, toys, magnetic latches on bags and cupboards, and credit/debit card strips. We can build simple things with magnets: a hanging compass, a magnet maze, or a paperclip lifter. Magnets should be kept away from electronic items like watches and TVs.

concepts.name: How Do We Measure?
concepts.description: Long ago, people measured length using parts of the body — handspan, foot, cubit (elbow to fingertip), and pace. The problem is that these vary from person to person, so the same measurement gave different answers. To fix this, the world agreed on standard units that everyone uses. This way, a 'metre' or a 'centimetre' means the same length to anyone, anywhere.

concepts.name: Standard Units
concepts.description: The International System of Units (SI) provides standard units accepted worldwide. The SI unit of length is the metre (m). Smaller units: centimetre (cm) and millimetre (mm). Larger unit: kilometre (km). 1 metre = 100 cm = 1000 mm; 1 km = 1000 m. We use different units for different distances — millimetres for a pencil tip, centimetres for a notebook, metres for a room, kilometres for a city.

concepts.name: Correct Way of Measuring Length
concepts.description: To measure length correctly: place the ruler flat along the object so that the zero mark is at one end of the object; read the number at the other end at eye level (looking straight down to avoid parallax error). If the zero mark of the ruler is broken or worn, start from a clear mark and subtract. Use the right tool — a ruler for short straight things, a measuring tape for longer or curved things.

concepts.name: Measuring the Length of a Curved Line
concepts.description: Curved lines (like the edge of a leaf or a winding road on a map) cannot be measured directly with a straight ruler. One way: place a thread along the curve carefully, mark the end points, then straighten the thread and measure with a ruler. Another way: use a flexible measuring tape. Both methods give the length of the curve.

concepts.name: Describing Position
concepts.description: To describe where something is, we need a reference point — something we can compare its position to. 'The shop is 200 m from the school' uses the school as reference. 'The book is on the second shelf, third from the left' uses the shelf and the leftmost book as references. Without a reference, position has no meaning.

concepts.name: Moving Things
concepts.description: An object is in motion when its position changes with time — relative to a reference point. A bus moving on the road, the hands of a clock, a swinging pendulum, a falling leaf — all are in motion. An object that does not change position is at rest. Whether something is in motion or at rest depends on the chosen reference — a passenger sitting in a moving bus is at rest relative to the bus, but in motion relative to the road.

concepts.name: Types of Motion
concepts.description: Motion can be of different types. Linear (rectilinear) motion: along a straight line — a falling stone, a marching column. Circular motion: along a circle — fan blades, hands of a clock, the Earth around the Sun. Periodic (oscillatory) motion: repeats after a fixed time — a swing, a pendulum. Some objects show more than one type at once — a bicycle wheel rotates while moving forward.

concepts.name: Observing Objects Around Us
concepts.description: The world around us is full of objects made of different materials — wood, metal, plastic, glass, cloth, paper, rubber, and more. The same object can be made from different materials (a chair of wood, plastic, or metal), and the same material can be used for many objects. Choosing the right material for each purpose depends on its properties.

concepts.name: How to Group Materials?
concepts.description: Materials can be grouped based on their properties. Some are hard (iron, glass), others soft (cotton, sponge). Some are shiny (metals), others dull (wood). Some are smooth, others rough. Some are transparent (let light pass through completely — clear glass), some translucent (let some light pass — frosted glass), some opaque (do not let light pass — wood, brick).

concepts.name: Different Properties of Materials
concepts.description: Properties help us identify and choose materials. Lustre — shines when polished (metals). Hardness — resists scratching (diamond, iron). Solubility — dissolves in water (salt, sugar yes; sand, oil no). Floats or sinks — depends on density. Magnetic or non-magnetic. Electrical and heat conductivity. Each property is tested with simple experiments.

concepts.name: What Is Matter?
concepts.description: All materials are made of matter. Matter is anything that has mass (a measure of how much stuff it contains) and takes up space (volume). Solids, liquids, and gases are all forms of matter. Mass is measured in grams (g) or kilograms (kg). Volume is measured in litres (L) or millilitres (mL). Even air has mass and takes up space — that is why a blown-up balloon is slightly heavier than an empty one.

concepts.name: Hot or Cold?
concepts.description: We often describe things as hot or cold by touching them. But touch can be misleading — a metal handle and a wooden handle in the same room feel different to touch even though they are at the same temperature. So our sense of hot and cold is relative and not always accurate. We need a reliable way to measure how hot or cold something is.

concepts.name: Temperature
concepts.description: Temperature is a measurement of how hot or cold something is. Unlike touch, it gives the same answer to everyone. Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius (°C) — the scale used in India and most of the world. Important reference points: ice water freezes at 0°C; water boils at 100°C; normal human body temperature is about 37°C; a hot summer day in Delhi can reach 45°C.

concepts.name: Measuring Temperature
concepts.description: A thermometer is the instrument used to measure temperature. A clinical thermometer measures human body temperature (range 35°C to 42°C); normal is about 37°C. A laboratory thermometer measures wider ranges (–10°C to 110°C). Always read the thermometer at eye level. Mercury thermometers are being replaced by safer digital thermometers. Place the thermometer in good contact with what you are measuring.

units.name: A Journey through States of Water

concepts.name: Investigating Water's Disappearing Act
concepts.description: Water left in an open container slowly disappears — it does not really vanish, but turns into water vapour and mixes into the air. This is called evaporation. We see evaporation when wet clothes dry, a wet floor dries, or a glass of water slowly empties on a hot day. Evaporation happens at all temperatures but is faster when it is hotter, drier, or windier.

concepts.name: Another Mystery — Where Do Water Drops Come From?
concepts.description: When we put cold water in a glass on a warm day, tiny water drops form on the outside of the glass. These drops do not come through the glass — they form because water vapour in the surrounding air cools down on the cold surface and turns back into liquid water. This process is called condensation. It is the opposite of evaporation.

concepts.name: What are the Different States of Water?
concepts.description: Water exists in three states. Solid (ice) — has fixed shape and volume. Liquid (water) — has fixed volume but takes the shape of its container. Gas (water vapour or steam) — has neither fixed shape nor fixed volume; it spreads out to fill any space. The same water moves between these three states without changing into a new substance.

concepts.name: How Can We Change the States of Water?
concepts.description: Adding heat or removing heat changes the state of water. Heating ice → it melts to liquid water (melting). Heating liquid water → it boils into water vapour (boiling/evaporation). Cooling water vapour → it becomes liquid (condensation). Cooling liquid water → it freezes to ice (freezing). These changes are reversible — water can be brought back to its original state.

concepts.name: How Can Water be Evaporated Faster or Slower?
concepts.description: Evaporation depends on several factors. Surface area: more surface area → faster evaporation (a saucer dries faster than a tall glass). Temperature: higher temperature → faster (clothes dry faster in sunshine). Wind: more wind → faster (clothes dry faster on a windy day). Humidity: drier air → faster. These factors explain why we hang clothes outside, and why a damp floor dries quickly with a fan on.

concepts.name: Cooling Effect of Evaporation
concepts.description: When water evaporates, it takes heat from its surroundings — this is why evaporation has a cooling effect. We sweat and the sweat evaporates from our skin to cool us down. Earthen pots (matkas) keep water cool because water seeps through the pot and evaporates from the outside. A pot-in-pot cooler uses the same idea to keep vegetables fresh without electricity.

concepts.name: How Do Clouds Give Us Rain?
concepts.description: The water cycle in nature is powered by the Sun. Sunlight heats water in oceans, rivers, and lakes — water evaporates and rises as vapour. As it rises, it cools and condenses into tiny droplets, forming clouds. When the droplets get heavy enough, they fall as rain (or snow or hail). The water collects in oceans, rivers, lakes, and underground — and the cycle continues.

units.name: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life

concepts.name: Why Do We Separate Mixtures?
concepts.description: Often the things we use in daily life are mixtures of two or more substances. We separate components from a mixture for many reasons — to remove harmful or useless impurities (stones from rice), to obtain useful components (salt from seawater, butter from milk), or to get the substance we want in pure form. Different methods are used depending on what is being separated.

concepts.name: Handpicking, Threshing and Winnowing
concepts.description: Handpicking is used to separate larger impurities by hand — like removing stones, husks, or insects from rice or dal. Threshing is the process of separating grains from stalks by beating the harvested crop on a hard surface or using a threshing machine. Winnowing separates lighter components (husk, chaff) from heavier grains using wind — the mixture is dropped from a height; wind blows the lighter husk away.

concepts.name: Sieving
concepts.description: Sieving separates components of different particle sizes using a sieve (a mesh). Smaller particles pass through the holes; larger particles stay back. Used to separate flour from bran, fine sand from gravel, or to remove lumps from flour. The size of the mesh decides what gets separated. At construction sites, large sieves separate fine sand from coarse pebbles.

concepts.name: Sedimentation, Decantation and Filtration
concepts.description: Sedimentation is the settling of insoluble heavy particles (sediment) at the bottom of a liquid when left undisturbed. Decantation is carefully pouring out the clear liquid from above without disturbing the sediment — used to separate mud from water. Filtration uses a filter (paper or cloth) to separate insoluble solids from a liquid; the liquid that passes through is the filtrate, the solid left behind is the residue.

concepts.name: Evaporation and Condensation
concepts.description: Evaporation separates a dissolved solid from a liquid. The liquid evaporates as vapour, leaving the solid behind. Common example: getting salt from seawater in salt pans — sunlight evaporates the water, leaving salt crystals. Condensation can be combined with evaporation to recover the liquid as well — the vapour is cooled to turn back into liquid. This is the principle of distillation.

concepts.name: Churning and Magnetic Separation
concepts.description: Churning separates a lighter component from a heavier liquid by stirring vigorously — used to obtain butter from curd (the lighter butter floats and is collected). Magnetic separation uses a magnet to pull out magnetic materials (like iron filings) from a non-magnetic mixture. Each method is chosen based on the difference in physical properties between the components being separated.

concepts.name: What Sets the Living Apart from the Non-living?
concepts.description: Living things share certain features that non-living things do not. They need food (nutrition), they breathe (respiration), they grow, they reproduce, they respond to stimuli (sensitivity), they excrete waste, and they show some kind of movement. A rock, a chair, water, or air do not show all these features. Some features (like growth or movement) can be tricky — even crystals grow, even cars move — but only living things show all features together.

concepts.name: Essential Conditions for Germination of a Seed
concepts.description: Germination is the process by which a seed grows into a tiny new plant (seedling). For germination, a seed needs three main conditions: water, air (oxygen), and the right temperature. Sunlight is not needed at the very start (the seed has stored food), but is needed soon after for the seedling to grow further. We can test these conditions with simple experiments using moong, gram, or rajma seeds.

concepts.name: Growth and Movement in Plants
concepts.description: Plants grow and also show movement, even though they do not walk like animals. The shoot grows upward (away from gravity, towards light); the root grows downward (into the soil). A plant kept near a window bends towards the light — this is called phototropism. The roots respond to gravity (geotropism) and to water (hydrotropism). Some flowers open in the morning and close at night.

concepts.name: Life Cycle of a Plant
concepts.description: The life cycle of a flowering plant: a seed germinates → seedling grows into a young plant → plant matures and flowers → flowers get pollinated and form fruits → fruits contain new seeds → seeds disperse and germinate to start the cycle again. Different plants take different lengths of time — a moong plant matures in weeks, a mango tree takes years. Each stage is essential.

concepts.name: Life Cycle of Animals
concepts.description: Animal life cycles vary widely. A butterfly: egg → larva (caterpillar) → pupa (cocoon) → adult butterfly — this is called metamorphosis. A frog: egg → tadpole (lives in water, has gills) → froglet → adult frog (lives on land, has lungs). Birds and most mammals are born or hatched as small versions of the adult and grow without major form changes. Each stage has a special role — feeding, growing, or reproducing.

concepts.name: Air
concepts.description: Air is all around us. It is a mixture of gases — nitrogen (about 78%), oxygen (about 21%), small amounts of carbon dioxide, water vapour, and other gases. Air has no colour, taste, or smell. We need oxygen from air to breathe; plants need carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. Wind is moving air, used in sailing boats, windmills, and to cool us down. Air also holds water vapour that gives us clouds and rain.

concepts.name: Water
concepts.description: Water is essential for all life. Sources include rain, rivers, lakes, ponds, oceans, springs, and groundwater (wells, tube wells). Only a small fraction of Earth's water is fresh and usable — most is salty seawater. We use water for drinking, cooking, washing, farming, industries, and electricity (hydroelectric power). Conserving water — fixing leaks, rainwater harvesting, drip irrigation — is everyone's responsibility.

concepts.name: Energy from the Sun
concepts.description: The Sun is the ultimate source of energy on Earth. It gives us light and heat. Plants use sunlight to make food (photosynthesis); we and other animals get energy by eating plants. Solar energy can be directly used in solar cookers, solar water heaters, and solar panels (which convert sunlight into electricity). Sunlight also dries clothes, evaporates water (driving the water cycle), and drives the weather.

concepts.name: Forests
concepts.description: Forests are areas with many trees and other plants growing together, sheltering a great variety of animals, birds, insects, and microorganisms. Forests give us oxygen, wood, fruits, gum, honey, medicines, and fibres. They prevent soil erosion, bring rain, store carbon, and home tribal communities. Cutting forests (deforestation) leads to floods, droughts, and loss of wildlife. Planting more trees (afforestation) helps restore them.

concepts.name: Soil, Rocks and Minerals
concepts.description: Soil is the loose top layer of Earth's surface, formed by the breaking down of rocks over long times by wind, water, and weather. Soil supports plant growth and is home to many small organisms. Rocks are solid masses of minerals; common types include sandstone, limestone, granite, and marble. Minerals (like iron, copper, gold, salt, and mica) come from rocks and are used to make many things — vessels, jewellery, tools, and electronic items.

concepts.name: Fossil Fuels
concepts.description: Fossil fuels — coal, petroleum (crude oil), and natural gas — formed underground from the remains of dead plants and animals buried millions of years ago. They are used as fuel for vehicles, generating electricity, and cooking (LPG). They release energy when burnt but also release carbon dioxide, contributing to air pollution and climate change. Fossil fuels take millions of years to form, so they will eventually run out — they are non-renewable.

concepts.name: Renewable and Non-renewable Resources
concepts.description: Natural resources are of two types. Renewable resources can be replenished naturally in a short time — sunlight, wind, water, forests (if managed well). Non-renewable resources take millions of years to form and will run out if used too much — fossil fuels, minerals. Using renewable resources (solar, wind, hydro) reduces pollution and saves non-renewable ones for the future.

concepts.name: Resources We Use — Saving for the Future
concepts.description: Every resource we use comes from nature. Wasting them — leaving lights on, leaving taps running, throwing away usable things, buying too much — is unfair to other people, other living things, and to future generations. Simple habits help: switch off when not in use, fix leaks, walk or cycle for short trips, recycle paper and plastic, eat less wasteful food. Taking care of nature's treasures is everyone's job.

concepts.name: Stars and Constellations
concepts.description: Stars are huge balls of hot glowing gas, like our Sun. They appear small because they are very far away. They seem to twinkle because their light passes through Earth's atmosphere. A constellation is a group of stars that appears to form a recognisable pattern in the sky — like Ursa Major (Saptarishi or the Big Dipper), Orion (Mriga), Cassiopeia, and the Southern Cross. Different cultures saw different shapes and gave different names.

concepts.name: Night Sky Watching
concepts.description: Watching the night sky is one of the oldest joys for humans. On a clear, moonless night, away from city lights, we can see thousands of stars, planets, and the band of the Milky Way. Tools that help: a sky map, a torch with red filter, binoculars, or a small telescope. Stars stay in the same patterns over a night, but the patterns shift slowly with seasons. Ancient sailors and travellers used the night sky to navigate.

concepts.name: Our Solar System
concepts.description: Our Solar System has the Sun at the centre with eight planets orbiting around it: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars (rocky inner planets), Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (gaseous outer planets). Many planets have moons; Earth has one. The Solar System also has dwarf planets (like Pluto), asteroids, and comets. The Sun's gravity holds everything in orbit. Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.

concepts.name: The Milky Way Galaxy
concepts.description: Our Sun and Solar System are just a tiny part of a vast galaxy called the Milky Way. A galaxy is a huge collection of billions of stars held together by gravity. The Milky Way contains hundreds of billions of stars. From Earth, on a clear dark night away from city lights, the Milky Way appears as a hazy band of light arching across the sky.

concepts.name: The Universe
concepts.description: The Universe is everything that exists — all stars, planets, galaxies, gas, dust, and even empty space. The Milky Way is just one of billions of galaxies in the universe. The universe is unimaginably large and is expanding. Space agencies like ISRO (India), NASA (USA), ESA (Europe) explore space using satellites, probes, and telescopes. India's recent successes include Chandrayaan and Aditya-L1.
